title: Groves v. John Wunder Co.
summary: A contractor’s deliberate failure to restore gravel land supported damages measured by the reasonable cost of the promised work, even though that cost exceeded the land’s market value; the case returned for a new trial.
notes:
The editors report a later $55,000 settlement and subsequent limited grading and sale of part of the land. Those later events inform the policy questions in the notes; they are not the court’s damages judgment or facts that supplied its original rationale.

The number that drives the debate: had Wunder graded the land as promised, the property would have been worth only $12,160, against a restoration cost above $60,000 (Groves v. John Wunder Co., 205 Minn. 163, 286 N.W. 235 (1939)).

The majority's rule: the proper measure of damages is the reasonable cost of performing the part of the contract that the defendant wilfully failed to complete; the dissent objected that a $60,000 award would enrich Groves beyond the value of his bargain.

sections.Parties: The plaintiff succeeded to the rights of S. J. Groves & Sons Company, the landowner and lessor. John Wunder Company was the lessee and gravel operator that promised to leave the property at an agreed grade.
sections.Material Facts:
Groves owned twenty-four acres of industrially zoned land on the outskirts of Minneapolis, together with a gravel-screening plant. Under a seven-year agreement made in 1927, Wunder paid $105,000, obtained the plant and the right to remove sand and gravel, and also removed Groves as a competitor. Wunder promised to leave the property at a uniform grade substantially corresponding to the roadway and to use overburden in establishing that grade.

Wunder deliberately removed the richest gravel and left the land rough and uneven. On the construction of the agreement accepted below, restoration would require moving approximately 288,495 cubic yards of overburden and cost more than $60,000. The land, even if properly restored, was valued at only $12,160. That disparity produced the dispute over the measure of compensation.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court awarded an amount a little above $15,000 including interest, using land value rather than the cost of completing the restoration. The plaintiff appealed. The Minnesota Supreme Court reversed and ordered a new trial in 1939. It also directed attention on remand to the proper construction of the grading obligation, which the parties had largely assumed rather than litigated.
sections.Issue: When the lessee deliberately fails to perform a promised land-restoration obligation, may compensation be limited to the land’s smaller market value instead of the cost of doing the promised work?
sections.Holding: The reasonable cost of the promised restoration was the proper damages measure under the majority’s approach. The court ordered a new trial; it did not enter a final award for the estimated $60,000.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority emphasized deliberate nonperformance and the owner’s right to buy a particular improvement. A party who has promised work cannot ordinarily reduce the obligation by arguing that the owner’s improvement is economically unattractive. Contract compensation concerns the promised performance, whereas damages for injury to land in tort commonly concern the land’s lost market value.

The majority also distinguished cases in which correcting minor defects would require tearing down a substantially completed structure. No such destruction was involved in completing the grading. It therefore declined to apply that version of the economic-waste exception. Wunder’s conduct also failed the good-faith substantial-performance premise that helped the builder in Jacob & Youngs.

The precise amount nevertheless depended on what the agreement required. The opinion questioned whether all the overburden really had to be removed from the premises, as assumed below, rather than used to produce an appropriate slope. That unresolved interpretation question explains the new trial.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: Groves makes the promised physical result central to expectation damages. Peevyhouse later adopts a different treatment of a similarly disproportionate restoration obligation.

topics.remedies: Chooses the cost of promised restoration over the smaller land-value measure.
topics.good-faith: Deliberate nonperformance affects the majority’s treatment of substantial performance and remedial fairness.
topics.interpretation: The scope of the grading promise remains an issue for the new trial.
topics.completion-damages: Groves is the leading cost-of-completion decision on the majority side of the cost-versus-value debate that Peevyhouse answers the other way.
topics.expectation-interest: The majority and dissent disagree over which measure actually puts Groves in the position performance would have, so the case defines what the expectation interest protects.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Olson, joined by Justice Holt, favored diminution in value absent evidence that the completed work would satisfy the promisee’s personal tastes. The dissent also disputed whether willfulness should change the measure of compensation.
